quests.hint: This is a long, polite request — keep a steady rhythm through the whole sentence.
quests.explanation: 'By the end of the week' sets a soft deadline, less strict than a specific day. This kind of polite, indirect request is typical in professional emails.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you send me the report by the end of the week?
quests.correctAnswer: Could you send me the report by the end of the week?

quests.hint: 'I'd appreciate it if' is a very polite way to make a request.
quests.explanation: 'I'd appreciate it if you could...' is a formal, courteous request structure often used in professional writing. It softens the request more than simply asking directly.
quests.textToSpeak: I'd appreciate it if you could confirm by Friday.
quests.correctAnswer: I'd appreciate it if you could confirm by Friday.

quests.hint: 'Would it be possible to' is an indirect, formal way to ask for something.
quests.explanation: Indirect questions like 'would it be possible to...' sound more polite than direct requests such as 'can we move it'. This kind of hedging is common in professional English.
quests.textToSpeak: Would it be possible to move our call to Tuesday?
quests.correctAnswer: Would it be possible to move our call to Tuesday?

quests.hint: 'She'd be' here means 'she would be', describing a planned near-future action.
quests.explanation: In reported speech, 'will' often changes to 'would' when the reporting verb is in the past. This shift is one of the key patterns in indirect speech.
quests.textToSpeak: She said that she'd be running a few minutes late.
quests.correctAnswer: She said that she'd be running a few minutes late.

quests.hint: 'Told me' needs a person as the object; 'said' usually doesn't.
quests.explanation: 'Tell' is always followed by a person, as in 'told me', while 'say' usually isn't, as in 'said that'. Mixing these two up is a very common learner error.
quests.textToSpeak: He told me he was thinking about changing jobs.
quests.correctAnswer: He told me he was thinking about changing jobs.

quests.hint: 'Had been cancelled' pushes the event back before the mentioning happened.
quests.explanation: The past perfect passive, 'had been cancelled', shows the cancellation happened before they mentioned it. This layering of tenses is typical in reported speech about past events.
quests.textToSpeak: They mentioned that the flight had been cancelled.
quests.correctAnswer: They mentioned that the flight had been cancelled.

quests.hint: 'Was built' is passive because the focus is on the bridge, not the builder.
quests.explanation: The passive voice is used here because we don't know or care who built the bridge — only the result matters. This is one of the most common reasons to choose the passive.
quests.textToSpeak: The bridge was built over a hundred years ago.
quests.correctAnswer: The bridge was built over a hundred years ago.

quests.hint: 'Is being renovated' is the present continuous passive — an action happening now.
quests.explanation: The present continuous passive combines 'is being' with a past participle to describe an ongoing action right now. 'At the moment' emphasises that it's happening currently.
quests.textToSpeak: This building is being renovated at the moment.
quests.correctAnswer: This building is being renovated at the moment.

quests.hint: 'Will be announced' is the future passive, focusing on the results, not the announcer.
quests.explanation: 'Will be announced' is future passive, useful when the person doing the announcing isn't important. 'Sometime next week' gives a flexible, approximate timeframe.
quests.textToSpeak: The results will be announced sometime next week.
quests.correctAnswer: The results will be announced sometime next week.

quests.hint: 'Although' introduces a contrast — pause briefly after the first clause.
quests.explanation: 'Although' connects two contrasting ideas within one sentence, similar to 'but' though slightly more formal. It can also start a sentence, unlike 'but'.
quests.textToSpeak: Although it was raining, we decided to go for a walk.
quests.correctAnswer: Although it was raining, we decided to go for a walk.

quests.hint: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or -ing form, never a full clause with 'that'.
quests.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase or -ing form, unlike 'although', which needs a full clause. Both express contrast, but their grammar afterwards is different.
quests.textToSpeak: Despite feeling nervous, she gave a confident presentation.
quests.correctAnswer: Despite feeling nervous, she gave a confident presentation.

quests.hint: 'However' here means 'no matter how' — stress it at the start.
quests.explanation: 'However' followed directly by an adjective means 'no matter how', a more advanced use than 'however' as a simple linking word. It adds emphasis to the contrast.
quests.textToSpeak: However busy I am, I always make time to exercise.
quests.correctAnswer: However busy I am, I always make time to exercise.

quests.hint: 'The way' is followed directly by a clause, with no extra 'that' needed.
quests.explanation: 'The way' can introduce a clause describing how something happens, without needing 'that' or 'in which'. This concise structure is common in natural spoken English.
quests.textToSpeak: Artificial intelligence is changing the way many people work.
quests.correctAnswer: Artificial intelligence is changing the way many people work.

quests.hint: 'To translate' shows purpose — the reason the app uses your voice.
quests.explanation: 'To' plus a verb often explains purpose, answering the question 'why'. This is one of the simplest and most useful ways to explain the function of something.
quests.textToSpeak: This app uses your voice to translate languages instantly.
quests.correctAnswer: This app uses your voice to translate languages instantly.

quests.hint: 'How we watch television' works like a noun, acting as the object of 'changed'.
quests.explanation: A clause starting with 'how' can act as the object of a verb, summarising a whole idea in a compact way. This is a flexible, natural structure in spoken English.
quests.textToSpeak: Streaming services have completely changed how we watch television.
quests.correctAnswer: Streaming services have completely changed how we watch television.

quests.hint: This is a positive statement, so the question tag is negative: 'haven't you'.
quests.explanation: Question tags flip the polarity of the main sentence: positive statements take negative tags, and negative statements take positive ones. They're used to check agreement or invite a response.
quests.textToSpeak: You've made real progress since we last spoke, haven't you?
quests.correctAnswer: You've made real progress since we last spoke, haven't you?

quests.hint: Your voice usually falls on the tag when you expect agreement.
quests.explanation: A falling tone on a question tag suggests you already expect the listener to agree, more like a comment than a real question. This small intonation choice changes the entire feel of the sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: It's a lovely evening, isn't it?
quests.correctAnswer: It's a lovely evening, isn't it?

quests.hint: The negative statement takes a positive tag: 'do you'.
quests.explanation: Since the main sentence is negative, the tag flips to positive, following the standard question tag pattern. This structure is one of the trickiest for learners to produce automatically.
quests.textToSpeak: You don't really believe that, do you?
quests.correctAnswer: You don't really believe that, do you?

quests.hint: 'Ended up' shows an unplanned result — stress it lightly.
quests.explanation: 'End up doing something' describes an unplanned or unexpected result, often used with a slightly regretful tone. It's a very natural way to describe how situations unfold.
quests.textToSpeak: We ended up arguing about something completely unimportant.
quests.correctAnswer: We ended up arguing about something completely unimportant.

quests.hint: 'Talk through' means to discuss something fully and carefully.
quests.explanation: 'Talk something through' means to discuss it thoroughly until it's understood or resolved. This phrasal verb suggests patience and care, useful in conflict resolution.
quests.textToSpeak: I think we should talk this through calmly.
quests.correctAnswer: I think we should talk this through calmly.

quests.hint: 'Sort out' means to resolve or organise — say it as a natural phrase.
quests.explanation: 'Sort out' is a flexible phrasal verb meaning to resolve or organise something, whether a problem, a schedule, or paperwork. It's extremely common in everyday British English.
quests.textToSpeak: It's better to sort out problems before they grow.
quests.correctAnswer: It's better to sort out problems before they grow.

quests.hint: 'Eating out' as a noun phrase pairs neatly with 'cooking at home' for comparison.
quests.explanation: Two gerund phrases, 'cooking at home' and 'eating out', are compared here using 'cheaper than'. This is a natural way to compare two habits or activities.
quests.textToSpeak: Cooking at home is generally cheaper than eating out.
quests.correctAnswer: Cooking at home is generally cheaper than eating out.

quests.hint: 'Plenty of' means a large, sufficient amount — say it smoothly as one phrase.
quests.explanation: 'Plenty of' works with both countable and uncountable nouns, unlike 'many' or 'much', which are more restricted. It's a flexible, common word for describing abundance.
quests.textToSpeak: A balanced diet includes plenty of fruit and vegetables.
quests.correctAnswer: A balanced diet includes plenty of fruit and vegetables.

quests.hint: 'Leave you tired' means 'cause you to become tired'.
quests.explanation: 'Leave' can mean 'cause someone to be in a certain state', as in 'leave you tired' or 'leave you confused'. This is a less obvious meaning of a very common verb.
quests.textToSpeak: Skipping breakfast can leave you tired by mid-morning.
quests.correctAnswer: Skipping breakfast can leave you tired by mid-morning.

quests.hint: 'Got delayed' is a more casual passive than 'was delayed'.
quests.explanation: 'Get' can replace 'be' in casual passive sentences, especially for unplanned or unlucky events, as in 'got delayed' or 'got stuck'. It sounds more natural in spoken English.
quests.textToSpeak: Our flight got delayed because of bad weather conditions.
quests.correctAnswer: Our flight got delayed because of bad weather conditions.

quests.hint: 'Had to' shows a past necessity — pronounce it smoothly as 'HAD-tuh'.
quests.explanation: 'Had to' expresses a past obligation that couldn't be avoided. 'Twice' is a useful frequency word meaning 'two times', placed right after the verb it describes.
quests.textToSpeak: We had to change trains twice to reach the coast.
quests.correctAnswer: We had to change trains twice to reach the coast.

quests.hint: 'At no extra cost' means for free, added on top of something else.
quests.explanation: 'At no extra cost' is a common phrase in travel and shopping contexts, meaning something was included for free. 'Upgrade' means to move to a better version of something.
quests.textToSpeak: The hotel upgraded our room at no extra cost.
quests.correctAnswer: The hotel upgraded our room at no extra cost.

quests.hint: List three items smoothly, with a short pause after each comma.
quests.explanation: This sentence lists three qualities using commas, with 'and' only before the final item. This standard pattern for listing keeps longer sentences clear and easy to follow.
quests.textToSpeak: Learning a language takes patience, practice, and plenty of mistakes.
quests.correctAnswer: Learning a language takes patience, practice, and plenty of mistakes.

quests.hint: 'The more... the more...' is a matching pair — balance the stress evenly.
quests.explanation: 'The more..., the more...' is a comparative structure showing two things increasing together. It's a natural, flexible pattern for describing cause and effect over time.
quests.textToSpeak: The more you practise speaking, the more confident you'll become.
quests.correctAnswer: The more you practise speaking, the more confident you'll become.

quests.hint: 'It's normal to' reassures the listener — say it warmly.
quests.explanation: 'It's normal to feel...' is a reassuring structure often used to encourage learners. 'Make an error' is a slightly more formal alternative to 'make a mistake'.
quests.textToSpeak: It's completely normal to feel embarrassed when you make an error.
quests.correctAnswer: It's completely normal to feel embarrassed when you make an error.
